title: Build a landing page generator
description: A system that turns a one-line idea into a full landing page with real copy in a single session.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

action.title: Action
action.content: A step an automation performs after the trigger fires — like 'send a Slack message' or 'create a Notion page.' One workflow can chain a dozen actions off a single trigger.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

script.title: Script
script.content: A small piece of code that tells a computer how to complete a task automatically — rename these files, pull this data, send that report. Scripts are deterministic: same input, same result, no model call needed. Claude writes them; you don't have to.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

hubspot.title: HubSpot
hubspot.content: A CRM and marketing platform used by sales, marketing, and customer success teams. Common target for AI automations — students connect it to draft outreach, enrich contacts, or sync data with other tools.

posthog.title: PostHog
posthog.content: An open-source product analytics platform that tracks user behavior, runs feature flags, and records session replays. Useful once a student's app has real users and they want to see what's actually being used.

frontend.title: Frontend
frontend.content: Everything a user sees and clicks in their browser — the buttons, text, layout, and styling. When Claude builds a portfolio site, the HTML and CSS it writes is the frontend.

grounding.title: Grounding
grounding.content: Feeding an AI real, current source material before it answers, so the response is based on facts instead of just training data. Copilot grounds in your organization's files; Gemini grounds in Google Search results. The main defense against hallucination.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Most landing pages fail because the copy is generic. The median dedicated landing page converts at roughly 4% across industries, per [Unbounce's Conversion Benchmark Report](https://unbounce.com/conversion-benchmark-report/), with SaaS pages typically landing below that median. This system takes a one-line idea and turns it into a full page, headline through FAQ, in a single session.

Personalized calls to [action](#tooltip-action) convert meaningfully better than generic buttons, per the same report. The build below forces every section back to one specific visitor before any copy gets written.

Run it as a [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) the first time you launch a page, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill) for every offer after that, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that drafts a page as soon as a new offer lands on your roadmap.
Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your visitor, the one action you want them to take, and where the page needs to live.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that takes a one-line description of my idea and produces a live landing page with real copy, not lorem ipsum. Ask me questions, one at a time, about who the page is for, what the single action I want them to take is, what makes my offer different from alternatives, and where the page needs to live once it's built. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming one visitor and one action before any copy exists keeps the page from drifting toward a general audience.

items: Where the page will be hosted, and whether that tool needs its own copy format.
Whether the page needs to connect to an email list or payment flow before the first draft.
How much of the visual design your AI tool owns versus a template you already have.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first in a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) by asking it to poke holes. Then gather what it calls for. Common [tool connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are your page builder or host (Framer, Webflow, Carrd), your email or waitlist tool (Mailchimp, ConvertKit, a form service), and an analytics tool to measure what happens after launch ([PostHog](#tooltip-posthog), Google Analytics). The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on your real idea and the visitor you have in mind. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Turn my one-line idea description into a complete landing page: headline, subhead, three benefit sections, one call to action, and FAQ.

Context: The idea is [one sentence]. The visitor is [specific person, e.g. "a solo bookkeeper deciding whether to try a new invoicing tool," not "small businesses"]. The one action I want them to take is [sign up, book a call, buy].

Rules:
- Write every benefit as an outcome for the visitor, never as a feature list.
- Keep the headline under 10 words.
- Do not invent a testimonial, statistic, or customer logo; leave a placeholder marked clearly where real proof needs to go.
- Match the single call to action across every section; never offer two competing next steps on one page.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: writing each benefit as an outcome forces the copy to describe what the visitor gets instead of listing what the product does.

children.text: **Review.** Check the draft against your scope. One visitor, one action, no invented proof?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what's off ("the headline talks to everyone, narrow it to the actual buyer") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Generate three headline variants and compare them.
Build a version of the page in a second language for a different market.
Add a returning-visitor variant that changes the headline for people who've seen the page before.
Turn the page copy into a [script](#tooltip-script) for a short video version of the same pitch.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft rubric and run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each landing page draft, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, offer or page, headline variant, conversion rate, and what I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks catch a page that reads well but sells to no one in particular, and the log columns make a headline's real performance visible across launches.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few launches straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. A page your AI tool writes in one pass reads like every other AI-written page unless it's [grounded](#tooltip-grounding) in real customer language from actual interviews. Publishing before the call to action gets checked against a real signup or payment flow means the conversion the page claims never happens.

items: [Unbounce, Conversion Benchmark Report](https://unbounce.com/conversion-benchmark-report/) — The median landing page conversion rate.
[HubSpot](#tooltip-hubspot), cited in Unbounce's Conversion Benchmark Report — The personalized call-to-action lift.
